children.translated_text: Having dispelled sloth and torpor here, and having gladdened the mind,
listen — I shall proclaim the <s>Udāna</s> (inspired utterance) spoken by the <s>Jina</s> (Conqueror).
Thus it was spoken by the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One), the all-knowing protector,
the compassionate sage (<s>ṛṣi</s>), the bearer of the final body.
Impermanent indeed are <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned things), subject to arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease — their pacification is happiness.
What joy, what delight can there be when all is blazing?
You have entered darkness — will you not seek a lamp?
These bones, cast aside, scattered in every direction,
pigeon-colored — seeing them here, what pleasure can there be?
From the very first night a human being dwells in the womb,
he departs without stopping, and once gone, does not return.
Some great people seen in the morning are not seen in the evening;
some great people seen in the evening are not seen in the morning.
How could any mortal there have confidence in life, thinking 'I am young'?
Even the young die — men and women, not just a few.
Some perish in the womb, others in the birthing chamber;
some while crawling, and some while running about.
Whether old, or young, or in the prime of life,
all depart in due order, like ripe fruit from its stalk.
Just as there is always the fear of falling for ripe fruits,
so there is always the fear of death for mortals who are born.
Just as vessels made of clay by a potter
all end in breaking — so is the life of mortals.
Just as when weaving upon the loom, whatever thread is woven in,
what remains to be woven becomes less — so is the life of mortals.
Just as also ... [text damaged]
[text damaged] ... such is the destruction — so is the life of mortals.
Just as a mountain stream flows and does not return,
so the lifespan of human beings goes and does not return.
Life is short and meager, and it is joined with suffering;
like a line drawn on water with a stick, it perishes swiftly.
Just as a cowherd drives cattle to pasture with his staff,
so do disease, old age, and death drive away the lifespan of mortals.
Days and nights pass by, and life is diminished;
the lifespan of mortals dwindles like water in a small stream.

Long is the night for one who is wakeful; long is the league for one who is weary;
long is <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence) for the foolish who do not know the true <s>Dharma</s>.
'I have sons, I have wealth' — thus the fool is tormented;
when even the self does not belong to the self, how can sons or wealth?

Many thousands of men and hundreds of women,
having gathered pleasures, come under the power of death.
All accumulations end in diminution; all elevations end in falling;
all unions end in separation; all life ends in death.
All beings shall die — life ends in death;
they shall go according to their <s>karma</s> (deeds), reaping the fruits of merit and sin.
Those of evil deeds go to hell; those of merit to a good destiny;
but others, cultivating the path here, will attain <s>nirvāṇa</s> (extinction), free from defilements.
Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a mountain cave —
there exists no place on this earth where one standing could escape death.
Those who have been here and those who will be — all shall depart, leaving the body;
the wise one, knowing this total loss, should live the <s>brahmacarya</s> (holy life), established in <s>Dharma</s>.
Having seen the aged, the diseased, and the dead whose consciousness has departed,
the wise one abandoned the bonds of the household — for the desires of the world are not easily given up.
Even splendid royal chariots decay, and indeed the body too comes to old age;
but the <s>Dharma</s> of the good does not come to old age — the good declare it among the good.
Shame on you, old age, vulgar one! You are the maker of ugliness;
for that delightful form has been crushed by old age.
Even one who lives a hundred years is bound for death;
old age strikes him, or disease, or the destroyer.
Always they proceed, never returning, day and night being worn away,
like fish exceedingly tormented, joined with the suffering of birth and death.

The lifespan, whether moving or standing still, by day and by night,
like the current of rivers, goes and does not return.
For those whose lifespan becomes shorter with the passing of each night and day,
like fish in diminishing water — what pleasure can there be for them?
This form is decrepit, a nest of disease, fragile;
this foul heap shall surely break apart — for life ends in death.
Before long, alas, this body shall lie upon the earth,
empty, devoid of consciousness, cast away like a useless log.
What use is this body, always oozing, always foul,
ever overwhelmed by disease, trembling with fear of old age and death?
With this foul body, afflicted and fragile,
attain the supreme peace, the unsurpassed <s>yogakṣema</s> (safety and welfare).
'Here I shall spend the rainy season, the winter, and the summer too' —
thus the fool plans, not seeing the obstacle.
That man, intoxicated with sons and cattle, with mind attached —
death carries him away, as a great flood carries away a sleeping village.
Sons are no protection, nor father, nor even kinsmen;
for one overcome by the destroyer, there is no protection from them.
'This I have done, this remains to be done, having done this, more will follow' —
thus while the mortal bustles about, old age and death crush him.
Therefore, always delighting in meditation, composed, ardent, seeing the end of birth and old age —
O <s>bhikṣus</s> (monks), having overcome <s>Māra</s> with his army, become those who have gone beyond birth and death.
2. Chapter on Desire (<s>Kāmavarga</s>)
O desire, I know your root — you arise from intention (<s>saṃkalpa</s>);
I shall not form any intention toward you — then you shall not exist for me.
From desires arises grief; from desires arises fear;
for those freed from desires, there is no grief — whence fear?
From pleasures arises grief; from pleasures arises fear;
for those freed from pleasures, there is no grief — whence fear?
Sweet at first but bitter in result, though welcomed,
desires burn the foolish, like a torch burns one who does not release it from the hand.
The noble ones say that bond is not strong which is made of iron, wood, or grass;
rather, the attachment of a passion-filled, dull-minded person to sons and wives —
that, the noble ones call a strong bond, tight on all sides, hard to loosen;
cutting even this, they go forth as renouncers, without longing, having abandoned the pleasure of desire.
Those beautiful things in the world are not desires — the desire of a person is the passionate intention;
the beautiful things remain just as they are in the world — but the wise ones discipline their longing.
Desires are not permanent among human beings; there are impermanent things to which the desirous are bound;
having abandoned those, for the sake of non-return, I declare the state beyond death.
One in whom desire has arisen, who is flowing with defilements, should become untroubled in mind;
one whose mind is not fettered to desires is called one whose stream flows upward.
Gradually, the wise one, moment by moment,
should blow away the impurity of the self, like a smith purifying silver.
Like a leather-worker cutting a sandal from hide,
whatever desires one abandons, to that extent happiness is attained.
If one desires all happiness, one should abandon all desires;
one who has abandoned all desires prospers in supreme happiness.
As long as one pursues desires, one attains no satisfaction of mind;
but those who, seeing the cessation, are truly satisfied — they are satisfied through wisdom.
Satisfaction through wisdom is superior; one is never satiated through desires;
the person satisfied through wisdom — craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) does not bring him under its power.
People greedy for desires, heedless — alas, they delight in <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness);
they do not see the danger while life is so short.
Enjoyment destroys the foolish, but not the seeker of the self;
the foolish person, through cravings for enjoyment, destroys himself and others.
Not even by a rain of gold coins is satisfaction with desires found;
'desires are of little savor and little happiness' — knowing this, the wise one
does not find delight even in divine pleasures;
one who delights in the destruction of craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) is always a disciple of the <s>Buddhas</s>.
Even if a mountain of gold were equal to <s>Himavat</s> (the Himalayas),
that wealth would not suffice for one person — knowing this, one should live with equanimity.
How could a being who knows suffering and its origin take delight in desires?
Knowing that attachment in the world is a thorn, the wise one should train for its removal.
3. Chapter on Craving (<s>Tṛṣṇāvarga</s>)
For a being who is agitated by discursive thoughts, of intense passion, seeing only the pleasant —
craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) increases further; indeed, this one makes a strong bond.
But one who delights in the calming of discursive thoughts, who always mindfully contemplates the unpleasant —
this one will abandon craving; indeed, one cuts the foul bond.
Beings, cast into the blind net of desire, covered by craving,
heedless, bound in bondage, like fish in the mouth of a trap,
they go toward old age and death, like a calf toward its mother for milk.
For a person who lives heedlessly, craving increases like a creeper;
he wanders from existence to existence, like a monkey in a forest seeking fruit.
Flowing attachments, affections, and joys arise for a being;
those who are attached to pleasure, seeking happiness — those mortals are subject to birth and old age.
Beings driven by cravings run about like a hare toward a snare;
bound by fetters and clinging to attachment, they go toward suffering again and again for a long time.
Beings tied by craving, with passionate minds, from existence to existence,
yoked by <s>Māra</s>'s yoke — those people have no safety and welfare;
they go toward old age and death — for the bonds are difficult to transcend.
But one who has abandoned craving here, free from craving in existence after existence,
the <s>bhikṣu</s> (monk) freed from craving, without longing, has attained complete <s>nirvāṇa</s> (extinction).
One who endures this vulgar craving in the world, so difficult to abandon —
sorrows increase for that person, like <s>bīraṇa</s> grass watered by rain.
But one who abandons this vulgar craving in the world, so difficult to abandon —
sorrows depart from him, like a drop of water from a lotus leaf. //
This indeed I say—may it be well for all of you who are gathered here:
dig out <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) with its root, as one who desires <s>uśīra</s> (fragrant root) [digs out] the <s>bīraṇa</s> grass;
when <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) has its root dug up, there is no sorrow—whence then fear? //
A person with <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) as his companion wanders a long path in expectation;
again and again he transmigrates, entering the womb again and again;
this becoming and becoming otherwise—coming and going in <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence). //
But having abandoned that <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) here, one free from craving in each existence—
that one does not transmigrate again, for craving indeed does not exist in him. //
By which gods and humans stand bound, desiring [pleasures]—
cross over this entanglement! Let the moment not pass you by!
For those who have let the moment pass grieve, consigned to the hells. //
For <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) is the cause, a river, an entanglement, a net ever spread forth like a swelling here;
having removed the creeper of thirst entirely, this suffering ceases again and again. //
Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again when its roots are undamaged,
so too, when the latent tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>) of craving are not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again. //
Just as a stake firmly driven in by oneself would destroy that very [person], empowered by force,
so too, the creepers of craving that arise from within lead living beings to their destruction. //
Having known this peril—that <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) is the origin of suffering—
a <s>bhikṣu</s> (mendicant), free from craving, without grasping, mindful, should wander forth. //
4. <s>Apramādavarga</s> (Chapter on Heedfulness)
Heedfulness (<s>apramāda</s>) is indeed the path to the deathless; heedlessness (<s>pramāda</s>) is the path of death;
the heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if always dead. //
Having understood this distinction of heedfulness, the wise one,
the noble one, should always rejoice in heedfulness, [dwelling in] his own domain. //
The heedful, the constant, those of ever-firm effort—
the steadfast ones touch <s>nirvāṇa</s>, the unsurpassed peace and security. //
When the wise one dispels heedlessness with heedfulness,
having ascended the terrace of wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), the sorrowless one [looks upon] the sorrowing people—
as one standing on a mountain looks down upon those standing on the ground, so the wise one regards the foolish. //
Through diligence, heedfulness, self-restraint, and self-control,
the intelligent one makes an island that no flood can overwhelm. //
Of one who is energetic, self-possessed, of pure mind, who acts with discernment,
who is self-controlled, who lives by the <s>Dharma</s>, who is heedful—the fame increases. //
Do not be heedless regarding the higher mind; train constantly in the stages of inner silence;
sorrows do not arise for one who is a protector, always pacified and self-possessed. //
One should not resort to inferior practices, nor dwell in heedlessness;
one should not delight in false views, nor be one who perpetuates the [attachment to] the world. //
One who possesses right view in abundance, even if worldly,
even through thousands of births, does not go to a bad destination. //
Fools, people of poor understanding, follow heedlessness;
but the intelligent one guards heedfulness as a wealthy merchant guards his treasure. //
Fools, people of poor understanding, follow heedlessness;
but the one who is always heedful and meditative attains the destruction of the <s>āsravas</s> (mental defilements). //
One should not pursue heedlessness, nor the praise of sensual pleasure;
the one who is always heedful and meditative attains unwavering happiness. //
This is not the time for heedlessness, when the destruction of the <s>āsravas</s> has not been attained;
<s>Māra</s> follows the heedless one, like a doe follows a lion. //
A heedless man who pursues the wives of others falls into four states:
the gain of demerit, an uncomfortable bed, blame as the third, and hell as the fourth. //
Seeing the gain of demerit, the evil destination, the slight pleasure of the frightened with the frightened,
and the blame, and the punishment of the king—one should avoid the wives of others. //
The gain of demerit, the evil destination, the slight pleasure of the frightened with the frightened,
and the king imposes a heavy punishment—after the breakup of the body, one sees [suffering] in the hells. //
With foresight should one do what one knows to be beneficial to oneself;
the wise one should not proceed slowly with the worries of a cart-driver. //
Just as a cart-driver, having left the smooth road, the highway,
arriving at an uneven road, with his axle broken, grieves greatly, //
so too, one who strays from <s>Dharma</s> and follows <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness),
the fool, having come under the power of death, grieves like one with a broken axle. //
What should be done is neglected, and what should not be done is done instead;
of the arrogant and heedless, the <s>āsravas</s> (defilements) increase;
the defilements grow in those who are far from the destruction of defilements. //
But those in whom mindfulness of the body is well undertaken constantly,
they do not do what should not be done, being constant doers of what should be done;
of the mindful and clearly comprehending, the <s>āsravas</s> (defilements) come to an end. //
One is not a bearer of <s>Dharma</s> merely by speaking much;
but one who, having heard even a little, touches the <s>Dharma</s> with the body,
that one indeed becomes a bearer of <s>Dharma</s>, who is not heedless regarding the <s>Dharma</s>. //
Even if a heedless person speaks much of the collected [teachings], not being a doer of them,
like a cowherd counting the cows of others, he has no share in the purpose of the <s>śrāmaṇya</s> (ascetic life). //
Even if one speaks little of the collected [teachings], if one practices in accordance with the <s>Dharma</s>,
having abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion—one becomes a sharer in the purpose of the <s>śrāmaṇya</s> (ascetic life). //
They praise heedfulness; heedlessness is always censured;
through heedfulness, <s>Maghavān</s> (<s>Indra</s>) attained the foremost position among the gods. //
The wise always praise heedfulness in duties;
the wise heedful one grasps both purposes. //
One purpose pertains to the visible <s>Dharma</s>, and the other to the future [life];
through the comprehension of both purposes, the steadfast one is called wise. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> (mendicant) devoted to heedfulness, seeing danger in heedlessness,
pulls himself out of difficulty, like an elephant sunk in mud. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> devoted to heedfulness, seeing danger in heedlessness,
shakes off evil states, as the wind [shakes off] leaves. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> devoted to heedfulness, seeing danger in heedlessness,
advances, burning every fetter small and great, like fire. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> devoted to heedfulness, seeing danger in heedlessness,
gradually touches the destruction of all fetters. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> devoted to heedfulness, seeing danger in heedlessness,
penetrates the peaceful state, the calming of <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations), the bliss [of <s>nirvāṇa</s>]. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> devoted to heedfulness, seeing danger in heedlessness,
is incapable of falling away—he is near to <s>nirvāṇa</s> itself. //
Arise! Strive! Train firmly for peace!
Forgetfulness, heedlessness, inactivity, and lack of self-control,
drowsiness, sloth, and lack of effort—these are obstacles to the training;
therefore awaken to this matter; let mindfulness not disappear within! //
One should rise up, not be heedless, and practice the <s>Dharma</s> of good conduct;
one who practices the <s>Dharma</s> sleeps happily in this world and the next. //
Be devoted to heedfulness, be virtuous, O <s>bhikṣus</s> (mendicants)!
With well-concentrated intentions, guard your own minds! //
Begin! Go forth! Yoke yourselves to the teaching of the <s>Buddha</s>!
Scatter the army of death, as an elephant [scatters] a hut of reeds! //
Whoever will be heedful in this <s>Dharma</s> and discipline,
having abandoned the cycle of birth in <s>saṃsāra</s>, will reach the end of suffering. //
5. <s>Priyavarga</s> (Chapter on the Dear)
From the dear ones arises sorrow; from the dear ones arises fear;
for those freed from the dear ones, there is no sorrow—whence then fear? //
From the dear ones arises sorrow; from the dear ones arises fear;
from the change of the dear ones, one even goes to madness. //
The sorrows, lamentations, and the manifold sufferings of the world—
all of this exists dependent on the dear; when there is no dear one, none of this would arise in any way. //
Therefore, happy and free from sorrow are those for whom there is nothing dear at all;
therefore, one seeking the sorrowless state should not make anything dear in the world of the living. //
May there never be union with the dear, nor ever with the unloved;
the not-seeing of the dear is suffering, and so is the seeing of the unloved. //
From the separation from the dear and from the union with the unloved,
intense sorrow arises, by which human beings are consumed. //
When a dear one has died and passed away, relatives standing together
grieve for a long time—painful indeed is the union with the dear. //
Therefore one should not make anything dear, for the state of endearment is evil;
there are no bonds for those for whom there is neither dear nor unloved.
Yoking oneself to the unyoked, and always unyoking from the yoked,
abandoning the [true] purpose, the one who grasps at the dear envies the one who has attained the purpose. //
The divine bodies, woven together with pleasing forms and pleasures, standing separately,
afflicted and wasted away, have gone under the power of the king of death. //
Those who, day and night, heedful, constantly abandon the dear—
they indeed dig up the root of evil, the bait of death so hard to overcome. //
The unwholesome in the guise of the wholesome, the unpleasant in the guise of the pleasant,
suffering in the guise of happiness—these crush the heedless. //
If one knows oneself to be dear, one should not yoke oneself with evil;
for happiness is not easily obtained by the doer of evil deeds. //
If one knows oneself to be dear, one should not yoke oneself with evil;
for happiness is easily obtained by the doer of good deeds. //
If one knows oneself to be dear, one should guard oneself well—
like a frontier city, deep-moated and firm;
the wise one should keep vigil during one of the three watches. //
If one knows oneself to be dear, one should protect oneself well—
like a frontier city, guarded within and without, firm;
guard yourselves in this way—let the moment not pass you by!
For those who have let the moment pass grieve, consigned to the hells. //
Having traversed all directions with the mind, one nowhere finds anything dearer than oneself;
likewise, each self is dear to others—therefore one who loves himself should not harm another. //
All tremble before punishment; to all, life is dear;
having made oneself the standard of comparison, one should neither kill nor cause to kill. //
Just as one who has been long traveling, having returned safely from afar,
relatives, well-wishers, and friends rejoice at his arrival— //
so too, a mortal who has done merit, having gone from this world to the next,
his merits welcome him, like relatives welcoming a dear one who has arrived. //
Therefore, accumulate a store of merits for the hereafter;
for merits in the other world are indeed the foundation for living beings. //
The gods praise merit and the one who practices equanimous conduct;
blameless here, after death he rejoices in heaven. //
One who abides in <s>Dharma</s>, endowed with virtue, possessed of moral shame, speaking truth—
People hold dear one who is a doer of good for himself;
And he becomes dear to others, for [good] is done for one's own sake as well;
He is praised in this visible world, and in the hereafter [he attains] a good destination. //
One should admonish, instruct, and restrain [others] from what is improper;
He becomes disliked by the wicked but dear to the good. //
The wicked and the good, departing from here, go to different destinations;
The wicked go to hell; the good are bound for heaven. //
6. <s>Śīlavarga</s> (Chapter on Moral Conduct)
The wise one should guard moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), aspiring for the threefold happiness:
Praise, acquisition of wealth, and rejoicing in heaven after death. //
Seeing these [three] rewards, the wise one should guard moral conduct;
The noble one, endowed with right view, obtains what is auspicious in the world. //
Pleasant is the undertaking of moral conduct — the body is not scorched;
One sleeps happily at night and rejoices upon awakening. //
Moral conduct is good until old age; faith is good when firmly established;
Wisdom is indeed the jewel of humans; merit is very hard for thieves to steal. //
Having performed meritorious deeds with wisdom, having given gifts with moral conduct,
Here and hereafter, he attains happiness. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> (monk) established in moral conduct, well-restrained in the senses,
Knowing moderation in food, and devoted to wakefulness —
Living thus with ardor, day and night, without sloth,
He is incapable of decline — he is indeed near <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. //
A <s>bhikṣu</s> established in moral conduct should cultivate the mind and wisdom;
Ardent and discerning always, he would attain the destruction of suffering. //
Therefore one should be constantly virtuous, a guardian of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration);
One should train in <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight), fully aware and mindful. //
He whose attachments are destroyed, whose pride is extinguished, who is free from the substrates of existence —
At the breaking up of the body, being wise, he is liberated and does not undergo further enumeration [of rebirths]. //
Moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), concentration (<s>samādhi</s>), and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) — for one in whom these are well cultivated,
He is of ultimate perfection, stainless, sorrowless, with birth destroyed. //
Freed from attachment, a forest-dweller who has attained perfect knowledge, free from the substrates of existence,
Having transcended the realm of <s>Māra</s>, he shines like the sun. //
For a <s>bhikṣu</s> who is restless, heedless, and outwardly directed,
Moral conduct, concentration, and wisdom do not reach fulfillment. //
It rains upon what is covered and does not rain upon what is open;
Therefore one should open what is covered — thus it will not rain upon it. //
Having seen this, the wise one should always train in the precepts;
One should quickly purify the path leading to <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. //
The fragrance of flowers does not travel against the wind — neither that of sandalwood, nor <s>tagara</s>, nor fire-born [incense];
But the fragrance of the good travels against the wind — a virtuous person pervades all directions. //
More than <s>tagara</s>, sandalwood, and also the <s>vārṣikā</s> flower and lotus,
Among all these kinds of fragrance, the fragrance of moral conduct is unsurpassed. //
Slight indeed is this fragrance that comes from <s>tagara</s> and sandalwood;
But the fragrance of the virtuous wafts even among the gods here;
Of those whose conduct is purified, who dwell in heedfulness,
<s>Māra</s> does not find the path of those liberated through right knowledge. //
This is the path leading to security; this is the path to purification;
Those who have entered it will abandon the bonds of <s>Māra</s>, those who meditate. //
7. <s>Sucaritavarga</s> (Chapter on Good Conduct)
One should guard against bodily transgression; one should be well-restrained in body;
Abandoning bodily misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the body. //
One should guard against verbal transgression; one should be restrained in speech;
Abandoning verbal misconduct, one should practice good conduct in speech. //
One should guard against mental transgression; one should be restrained in mind;
Abandoning mental misconduct, one should practice good conduct of mind. //
Having abandoned bodily misconduct and verbal misconduct,
Having abandoned mental misconduct and whatever else is connected with fault —
One should perform what is wholesome (<s>kuśala</s>) with the body, much that is wholesome with speech,
And one should perform what is wholesome with the mind — immeasurable, free from substrates. //
Having performed what is wholesome with body, speech, and mind,
Here and hereafter, he attains happiness. //
Non-violent indeed are the sages, always restrained in body;
They go to the imperishable state, where having gone, one does not grieve. //
Non-violent indeed are the sages, always well-restrained in speech;
They go to the imperishable state, where having gone, one does not grieve. //
Non-violent indeed are the sages, always restrained in mind;
They go to the imperishable state, where having gone, one does not grieve. //
The steadfast are restrained in body; the steadfast are well-restrained in speech;
The steadfast are restrained in mind; the steadfast are restrained in all respects;
They go to the imperishable state, where having gone, one does not grieve. //
Restraint of body is good; good is restraint of speech;
Restraint of mind is good; good is restraint in all respects;
A <s>bhikṣu</s> restrained in all respects is freed from all suffering. //
Guarded in speech, well-restrained in mind, one should not do what is unwholesome with the body;
Purifying these three bright paths of action, one would attain the path proclaimed by the sages. //
8. <s>Vācavarga</s> (Chapter on Speech)
A speaker of falsehood goes to hell, as does one who, having done a deed here, says 'I did not do it';
Both of them, after death, are declared equal — people of base conduct in the hereafter. //
For a person who is born, an axe is born in the mouth,
By which he cuts himself — speaking ill-spoken words. //
He who praises the blameworthy and blames those who are praiseworthy,
He accumulates that misfortune with his mouth; through that misfortune he finds no happiness. //

The miserly do not go to the world of the gods; fools do not praise giving;

One who is eager to listen gains wisdom, being discerning everywhere.

Impermanence, desire, craving, and diligence, which is dear,

Summary (<s>Uddāna</s>):
Impermanence, desire, craving, and diligence, which is dear,
virtue, good conduct, speech, action, and faith — these are the ten.
The ascetic, the path, honor, hostility, mindfulness, and the miscellaneous —
water, flower, and the horse, together with anger — these are the ten.
Likewise, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, learning, the self, the summary, and friendship as fifth,
<s>Nirvāṇa</s>, seeing, evil, and the yoke chapter together with happiness.
Mind, the <s>bhikṣu</s>, and the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> — thirty-three [chapters] are remembered;
the chapters are complete, and the summary — rightly spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One.
